strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical problem: extending VLA-based navigation to full 360° surround-view perception rather than the single front-facing camera used by prior VLA navigation methods, which is a meaningful architectural contribution with clear real-world motivation (thin obstacles, squeezing through gaps, dynamic obstacle avoidance from any direction).

The teacher-student distillation design that trains three specialized RL experts (reaching, squeezing, avoiding) with privileged depth information and distills them into a single RGB-only VLA policy is a sensible way to combine the strengths of RL (access to privileged sensing, capability specialization) and VLA (generalization, robustness to sim-to-real gap) and is reasonably well described.

The capability-balanced data aggregation strategy (weighted travel time gap-based proportional sampling) is a reasonable and mildly novel technical contribution for online DAgger-style fine-tuning across heterogeneous tasks, and the ablation in Fig. 6 shows a plausible benefit over unbalanced aggregation.

The experimental evaluation includes both simulation (against relevant recent baselines: iPlanner, ViPlanner, NavDP) and a reasonably diverse set of real-world scenarios (narrow corridors, thin obstacles, dynamic pedestrians/wheelchairs, cluttered/transparent objects), and the method shows consistent improvements over baselines in SR/CR/WTT across all tested simulation scenes.

The ablation studies (individual vs mixed-capability training, online iteration progress) provide some insight into why combining multiple experts helps and support the claimed synergistic effect of multi-capability training, which is an interesting and non-trivial empirical finding.

The system achieves a practically relevant inference rate (~7Hz) with a 7B-parameter LLM backbone, which is a solid engineering contribution for real-time deployment of VLA policies on a real quadruped robot.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons appear somewhat unfair: iPlanner, ViPlanner, and NavDP are single-camera/front-view methods evaluated against MM-Nav's 4-camera 360° system, so the large performance gap may be substantially attributable to the sensor configuration difference rather than the proposed multi-expert distillation and balancing method; a controlled comparison (e.g., feeding baselines all four views, or comparing against a single-expert/single-view ablation of MM-Nav itself) would better isolate the source of improvement.

There is no comparison to other VLA-based navigation baselines (e.g., NaVid, Uni-NaVid, X-Nav, COMPASS) that are extensively discussed in related work; the only baselines evaluated quantitatively are classical planning-based (iPlanner, ViPlanner) and a diffusion policy (NavDP), leaving the core claim of VLA superiority over other VLA navigation methods unsubstantiated experimentally.

Real-world evaluation is entirely qualitative (Fig. 1, Fig. 5, prose description) with no quantitative success rate, collision rate, or comparison against baselines in real environments, despite the abstract's emphasis on 'extensive real-world experiments' confirming effectiveness; this weakens the evidentiary support for the sim-to-real transfer claims.

Key design choices lack ablation or justification: e.g., the specific loss weight β=5, the choice α=0.3 for smoothing in the capability-balancing formula, ϵ=0.1, and the reward coefficients for RL experts are stated but not justified or ablated, raising reproducibility and sensitivity concerns.

The claim that the VLA student 'outperforms the RL teachers' is presented as a key novel finding, but this could partly stem from the RL experts being under-tuned/limited by scene-specific overfitting or the shared MLP architecture bottleneck (128-256-512 hidden units) rather than a fundamental synergy effect; alternative explanations (e.g., simply more total training data seen by VLA vs. RL) are not ruled out.

No statistical significance / variance reporting (e.g., std over multiple seeds/runs) is given for the 100-episode evaluations, making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., 47% vs 23% SR in Mixed) are robust or could partly reflect stochastic simulation variance.

The paper does not discuss failure cases or limitations of MM-Nav in depth (e.g., where does 20-32% collision rate in Squeezing/Avoiding scenes come from, what specific failure modes remain), which would be valuable given the safety-critical nature of navigation.

The compute/data cost of training three separate RL experts plus iterative online VLA fine-tuning with a 7B LLM (40+ GPU-hours per initial stage plus multiple 2-hour iterations on 8xH100) is significant, and no discussion of scalability to additional capabilities or environments is provided, raising questions about how this approach would extend beyond the three hand-designed capabilities.

strengths: Well-motivated multi-expert RL-to-VLA distillation framework that decomposes visual navigation into three complementary, hard-to-collect-in-reality capabilities (reaching, squeezing, avoiding), providing a practical route to obtain diverse, safety-critical training data without risking real-world collisions.

Clean multi-view (360°) VLA architecture with an efficient tokenization/pooling design that achieves 7 Hz inference with a 7B-parameter backbone, a non-trivial engineering contribution given the added camera streams.

Thorough and largely convincing experimental validation: results on the public InternVLA-N1 System-1 benchmark (state-of-the-art SR/SPL), a custom IsaacLab benchmark with capability-specific and mixed scenes, and extensive qualitative real-world deployments across four distinct hard scenarios (thin-wire avoidance, cluttered/transparent corridors, pedestrian avoidance, low-light outdoor).

Sensible and empirically validated capability-balanced data aggregation scheme (weighted-travel-time gap-based sampling) with clear ablations showing it outperforms unbalanced training in convergence speed/stability.

Good diagnostic analyses beyond headline numbers: UMAP visualization of VLM latent states shows that VQA co-training measurably closes the sim-to-real distribution gap, and the single- vs multi-view and expert-combination ablations (Table 3) support the claimed synergistic benefit of multi-capability training.
Detailed appendix (RL formulation, reward decomposition, environment construction, hyperparameters) supports reproducibility of the RL-expert component.
weaknesses: Some comparisons may be unfair to the RL experts: they are evaluated out-of-domain (e.g., on InternVLA-N1 benchmark scenes) where their privileged-depth policies were never trained, which inflates the apparent 'VLA surpasses RL teacher' narrative; a same-domain comparison would better isolate the distillation/synergy effect from simple domain-gap artifacts.

Real-world evaluation is largely qualitative; the only quantitative real-world numbers are a small ablation (20 trials/scenario) on VQA co-training, with no head-to-head real-world comparison against other visual navigation baselines (ViNT, NoMaD, NavDP, etc.) that are discussed in Related Work, limiting the strength of the sim-to-real transfer claim.

The three hand-designed capabilities (reaching/squeezing/avoiding) are a useful but somewhat coarse decomposition of navigation skill space; it is unclear how well this taxonomy scales to more diverse real-world behaviors not captured by these three synthetic scene archetypes, and the 'Mixed' test scene, while helpful, is still simulation-only.

Several heuristic hyperparameters (reward coefficients α, β, γ, δ, regularization ε, smoothing exponent α=0.3 in Eq. 6) are introduced with limited principled justification or sensitivity analysis, raising reproducibility/robustness concerns for the capability-balancing mechanism.

Deployment relies on an off-board RTX 5090 server for inference rather than onboard compute, which somewhat undercuts the practical real-time/robotics-deployment framing despite the reported 7 Hz figure.

Tables report single-run success rates without variance/confidence intervals, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains (e.g., +15.9 SR points over the best baseline).

Description of the real-world VQA dataset (source, scale beyond '300k/100k' figures, content diversity) is relatively thin, making it hard to judge exactly what real-world knowledge is being transferred and how reproducible this component is.
